ow widely accept the idea that the geomagnetic field has reversed itself in the geological past. This hypothesis has become more and more con- vincing as additional paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data have accumulated. However, there still remains the possibility of naturally occurring self-reversal of the magnetic polarity in some rocks. Very few cases have been reported in which the self-reversing properties of rock-forming ferrimagnetic minerals could be demonstrated in the laboratory (Uyeda, 1958; Carmichael, 1959; Havard and Lewis, 1965), but some of the self-reversal mechanisms may not be reproducible on a laboratory time scale (Neel, 1951; Verhoogen, 1956). Ade-Hall (1964) reported a fairly strong correlation between the polarity of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) and the stage of alteration or oxidation of minerals in basalt lavas of Mull, Scotland. Although paleomagnetic studies did not reveal systematic differ- ences between normal and reversed lava flows (Wilson, 1964), Ade-Hall claimed on the basis of his petrological observations that a self-reversal mechanism might be responsible for the NRM of the reversed flows. Wilson and Watkins (1967) claim a correlation between petro- graphy and polarity but agree that field reversals have occurred. Larson and Str

Conclusions The results of the present investigation are clearly in favor of the hypothesis of field reversal. (1) Samples from the contact sedimentary zones have the same directions of NRM as those of the overlying lavas. (2) Stability of NRM of both normal and reversed samples is relatively high and shows similar scatter. (3) No correlation is found between the polarity of NRM and the magnetic and petro- graphic properties of the ferrimagnetic minerals contained in the rocks. The results of these studies have strongly supported the continental drift theory of the Indian land- mass between Jurassic to Miocene times from the southern hemisphere to its present position in the northern hemisphere. In addition to continental drift the results of paleomagnetic studies on Deccan traps have giv- en a strong evidence in support of geomagnetic field reversal during Upper Cretaceous times. The Deccan traps have been classified on the basis of paleomagnetic results into Lower and Upper Deccan traps, the Lower ones being re- versely magnetized and the upper ones being normal. The plane of distinction between the normal and the reversed rocks seems to lie somewhere near an elevation of about 2000 ft above mean sea level [5]. Hargraves (1959) obtained a field vector for the Lac Tio ilmenite deposit, but not knowing whether the Lac Tio deposit had remained undisturbed since its magnetization, he did not attempt the calculation of a "pole position". Detailed petrological descriptions of the dykes have been given by Kindle (1933) and by Collins (1935), among others. The anor- thosite mountain is then regarded as part of the area of central uplift com- parable with other supposed meteorite craters on the earth, the moon, and Mars, and the dacitic material is the product of shock melting and ejection from the region of impact (Dence 1965). GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING The circular feature is set in an area of Precambrian foliated gneisses, basic intrusive rocks, and metasediments of the Grenville (structural) Province. Most of the area within the twin lakes is covered by the dacitic material, which is in places more than 700 ft thick, and lies nearly horizontally on the basement. Their results indicated a counterclockwise rotation of Spain (GIRDLER, 1965), postulated previously by several authors (DE TOIT, 1937; CAREV, 1958; BULLARD et al., 1965). Recent investigations (VAN DER VOO, 1967, and th

(1962, 1963) yielded virtual Permo-Triassic pole positions that were different from those for stable (extra alpine) Europe. Their results indicated a counterclockwise rotation of Spain (GIRDLER, 1965), postulated previously by several authors (DE TOIT, 1937; CAREV, 1958; BULLARD et al., 1965). Recent investigations (VAN DER VOO, 1967, and the present paper) on volcanic and sedimentary rocks lead to firmer based palaeomagnetic evidence for the rotation of the Iberian peninsula. INTRODUCTION As part of a palaeomagnetic investigation program carried out by members of the State University of Utrecht, 94 samples from the Sierra del Cadi (Huesca province, Spain) were taken in the summer of 1966 in order to obtain paleD- magnetic data from the eastern Pyrenees. Some years ago similar investigations in the Spanish Pyrenees by VAN DER LINGEN (1960) and SCHWARZ (1962, 1963) yielded virtual Permo-Triassic pole positions that were different from those for stable (extra alpine) Europe. Their results indicated a counterclockwise rotation of Spain (GIRDLER, 1965), postulated previously by several authors (DE TOIT, 1937; CAREV, 1958; BULLARD et al., 1965). During treatment with a.c. magnetic fields with strengthes up to values varying between 750 and 1,500 Oe a component is eliminated which conforms to the present-day geomagnetic field and thus is secondary. Between 1,500 and 3,000 Oe the demagnetization reveals another component with a direction similar for all samples; the latter is the characteristic component (plotted in stereographic projection in Fig.3C). Five more samples have been taken from one dacitic flow near the railway station of Almadenejos, situated at 11.5 km east of Almad6n. METHODS OF RESEARCH The samples were sawn to approximately equidimensional shape and embed- ded in their correct orientation in cubes of paraffin with 10-cm edges; thereupon directions and intensities were measured on the Utrecht astatic magnetometers. The natural remanent magnetization (N.R.M.) of all samples was analysed by progressive demagnetization with a.c. magnetic fields up to 3,000 Oe (peak value). For an extensive description of the methods of measurement and the analysis of the N.R.M. with the aid of a.c. magnetic field demagnetization the reader is referred to As and ZIJDERVELD (1958), AS (1960), and ZIJDERVELD (1967a). The numerical data thus obtained are summarized in Table I and II, and Fig.3, 5 and 7 show the data plotted in stereographic projection. The correction for the geomagnetic variation has been applied. These ages differ radically from the value of about 1200 SYMONS: PALEOMAGNETISM OF PRECAMBRIAN ROCKS 1167 m.y. postulated by Strangway (1964) on the basis of the rate of decay of stable remanence intensity. The lack of evidence of significant structural deformation, the underlying horizontal sediments, and the fresh appearance of the diabase favor retention of an unaltered primary remanence. The remanence of the diabase samples is associated with titanomagnetite, which is the only significant ferromagnetic mineral (Satterly 1928). One sample (number 1) of Nipissing diabase from near the surface had an extremely intense n.r.m., anomalous remanence directions and an abnormally high Koenigsberger ratio. It may have been lightning struck and hence was discarded. This evidence for remanence stability suggests that the calculated pole position (74.4OE, ll.gON) reliably reflects the earth's field at the time the diabase was intruded. These magnetic properties suggest that the remanence of the upper slate member is composed of two or more components. Probably, the primary d.r.m. or c.r.m. of the upper slates has been mostly obliterated by contact metamorphism during intrusion of the Nipissing sill, which impressed a secondary remanence on the slates. This secondary remanence is probably a t.r.m. associated with heating to a temperature of about 500 f 75 "C, which is the probable Curie Point range for the primary ferromagnetic minerals, or possibly a c.r.m. associated with hydrothermal chemical reactions. The Veldurti hematite deposits occupy a prominent zone of faulting which has been called the Gunny gull fault. The fault zone cuts across the Archean gneisses and basal formations of the Cuddapah System. The iron ore deposits form low hillocks or ridges whose general trend is E-W to ENE-WSW. 499 500 R. K. Samples from sixty sites are regarded as reliable indicators of the polarity of remanence but only sixteen sites are regarded as reliable indicators of the actual direction of the past geomagnetic field. Normal and reversed

Palaeomagnetic results from the Hawaiian Islands have been described earlier (Doell & Cox 1961,1963, Tarling 1965) and the presence of reversals of magnetization in Samoa has been noted previously (Tarling 1962). The Samoan volcanics form part of the oceanic basalt suite of rocks while the Tongan Islands, lying along the Andesite Line, are representative of a 'continental' or 'subcontinental' environment. from Samoa and Tonga were examined as part of an investigation of the variation of the geomagnetic field during the last few million years in islands in and around the margin of the Pacific Ocean. In particular it was hoped (a) to estimate the magnitude of secular variation in this region of slow change during historic times, (b) to test the hypothesis of world-wide reversals of the geomagnetic field and to use such reversals for geo- logical correlation in an area where standard stratigraphical techniques are difficult to apply, and (c) to test the axial dipole hypothesis of the average geomagnetic field during the late Cainozoic. Palaeomagnetic results from the Hawaiian Islands have been described earlier (Doell & Cox 1961,1963, Tarling 1965) and the presence of reversals of magnetization in Samoa has been noted previously (Tarling 1962). The Samoan and Tongan Islands are in close proximity but these islands are representative of two distinct geological environments. The Samoan volcanics form part of the oceanic basalt suite of rocks while the Tongan Islands, lying along the Andesite Line, are representative of a 'continental' or 'subcontinental' environment. Therefore each island group is described separately following an outline of the methods used. * Present address: Department

from Samoa and Tonga were examined as part of an investigation of the variation of the geomagnetic field during the last few million years in islands in and around the margin of the Pacific Ocean. In particular it was hoped (a) to estimate the magnitude of secular variation in this region of slow change during historic times, (b) to test the hypothesis of world-wide reversals of the geomagnetic field and to use such reversals for geo- logical correlation in an area where standard stratigraphical techniques are difficult to apply, and (c) to test the axial dipole hypothesis of the average geomagnetic field during the late Cainozoic. Palaeomagnetic results from the Hawaiian Islands have been described earlier (Doell & Cox 1961,1963, Tarling 1965) and the presence of reversals of magnetization in Samoa has been noted previously (Tarling 1962). The Samoan and Tongan Islands are in close proximity but these islands are representative of two distinct geological environments. The Samoan volcanics form part of the oceanic basalt suite of rocks while the Tongan Islands, lying along the Andesite Line, are representative of a 'continental' or 'subcontinental' environment. Introduction The Umkondo System lies southeast of Southern Rhodesia on the border of MoGambique. Descriptions of various parts of the Umkondo System have been given by Swift et al. McElhinny (Received 1965 February 16) Summary The mean direction of magnetization of samples collected from nine sites in the Umkondo lavas shows no significant difference from that of the Umkondo dolerites after demagnetization in alternating magnetic fields. This supports the contention of geologists that the dolerites are the intrusive phase of the lavas. The lavas exhibit considerably greater dispersion than the dolerites and it seems possible that the sampling of' the latter may have been insufficient to average out secular variation. The combined data for the lavas and the dolerites gives an estimate of the angular dispersion of the geomagnetic field in Umkondo times which is in good agreement with that calculated fo

avas exhibit considerably greater dispersion than the dolerites and it seems possible that the sampling of' the latter may have been insufficient to average out secular variation. The combined data for the lavas and the dolerites gives an estimate of the angular dispersion of the geomagnetic field in Umkondo times which is in good agreement with that calculated for the present field. 1. Introduction The Umkondo System lies southeast of Southern Rhodesia on the border of MoGambique. Descriptions of various parts of the Umkondo System have been given by Swift et al. (1953), Swift (1962) and Watson (1964). It rests upon the base- ment granite of the Rhodesian Shield and is presumed to be Pre-Cambrian in age. In the extreme southeast it is overlain unconformably by beds of the Karroo System. Since it is completely isolated from other Pre-Cambrian Systems in Rhodesia its age has thus been a matter of some speculation. Fig. 1 shows a geological map of the Umkondo System, which consists of the Calcareous Series composed of a basal arkose and limestones about 800ft thick. This is overlain by the Lower Argillaceous Series of grey shales and siltstones about 800ft thick, followed by the Quartzite Series of massive dark grey crystalline quartzitic sandstones some 3 000 ft thick.

The latter is roughly parallel to the supposed direction of the Permian geomagnetic field, and is considered to have been induced by moderate heating during burial at about the time of the Appalachian orogeny. pecimens which initially had widely scattered magnetizations yielded consistent directions when measured at high enough temperatures. The gabbro is intruded by the Gabcrones granite, and samples from two sites in the granite show almost horizontal magnetization. On initial measurement gabbro samples collected near the contact yield direc- tions close to those of the granite, which suggests that the gabbro was reheated at the time of emplacement of the granite (2350 m.y. ago). McEIHNNY  Physics Department, University College oJ Rhodesia Salisbury, Rhodesia Samples have been collected from eleven sites in the Modipe gabbro which crops out on the border of Bechuanaland and South Africa. After partial demagnetization in alternating magnetic fields, ten of these sites give almost vertical directions of magnetization, forming a close group which corresponds to a palcomagnetic pole at 33øS, 31øE. The gabbro is intruded by the Gabcrones granite, and samples from two sites in the granite show almost horizontal magnetization. On initial measurement gabbro samples collected near the contact yield direc- tions close to those of the granite, which suggests that the gabbro was reheated at the time of emplacement of the granite (2350 m.y. ago). After magnetic cleaning, some of these samples give directions which agree with those at the other gabbro sites. Together with detailed alter- nating field and thermal demagnetization studies, this agreement provides strong evidence that the magnetically cleaned directions are those of the TRM acquired when the gabbro originally cooled. The gabbro has an age of approximately 2600 m.y. and is to date the oldest rock unit that has been studied palcomagnetically; the results imply the existence of a geo- magnetic field in this early stage of the earth's history. Alternating field demagnetization ex- periments indicate that some of the magnetic grains have very high coercivities. Thermal demagnetization and IRM studies exclude the presence of hematite and show that the mag- netic mineral present is magnetite. A potassium-argon whole-rock age determination has confirmed the Trias- sic age assignment to the dike rocks. These mountains, which are char- acterized by rolling, knob-like hills of Pre- cambrian igneous rocks, stand some 500 to 1700 feet in relief above the surrounding terrain. The igneous rocks of this area have been ex- tensively investigated petrologically by Tolman and Robertson [1960] and others. The present work represents the first extensive effort to in- vestigate the paleomagnetic properties of these relatively undisturbed Precambrian rocks. Geology and sampling. The Precambrian igneous rocks of the St. Francois Mountains fall into three major petrologic groups: a variegated series of granites, a system of basic intrusives of gabbroic composition, and a group of intrusive and extrusive felsites of rhyolitic composition. Consider, for example, the palcomagnetic data from the Pololu volcanic series (Figures 1 and 12), which display the following unusual characteristics. Farther up in the section, there appear to be several more oscillations be- tween these two directions. This may correspond to a real, if unusual, property of the geomag- netic field. However, the following model would also explain these data in terms of reheating. All of the flows may have cooled originally in a short time interval when the earth's field had the nondipole direction. Subsequently the pile was buried and reheated to, say, 300øC at a time when the field had changed to an axial dipole direction. In our earlier study of historic Hawaiian lava flows we showed that an accuracy of 3 ø to 5 ø was possible if five to eight samples were collected from each flow. However, the older Hawaiian lavas are several hundred thousand years older than the historic flows, and during this time some of the original magnetization may have been lost or new components of magnetiza- tion may have been added. Some of the older lavas were initially buried before being exposed by erosion, so that the possibility of remagnetiza- tion through reheating must be considered. Rocks of Triassic age in Pennsylvania are exposed in a belt approxi- mately 225 km long and 6 to 50 km wide which trends approximately east-northeast across the southeastern corner of the state. This belt of exposures is part of a longer outcrop belt, the Gettysburg-Newark basin, which is the largest of the Triassic basins of the eastern United States. To date, sampling has been confined to the southwestern three-quarters of the Pennsyl- vania part of this belt, from the Maryland border to a point several miles southeast of Birdsboro (see Figure 1). Most, explanations for this homoclinal structure involve gradual subsidence of the Triassic basin during sedimentation, culminating in block faulting immediately after intrusion of the diabase [Stose, 1949; Willard et al., 1959, pp. 222-225]. During the 1962 field season specimens were collected from red horizons of Ecca age (lower Permian) from the Galula coalfield, the Songwe-Kiwira coalfield, and the Ketewaka-Mchuchuma coalfield. Farther to the south in Africa the rocks of Ecca age do not contain red horizons, and attempts to obtain paleomagnetic information for this region have been unsuccessful [Nairn, 1960; Graham, 1961]. Field work was severely limited by the lack of roads, which limited accessibility to outcrops. Artificial exposures such as road cuts and quar- ries are practically nonexistent. The most useful exposures proved to be the beds of dry rivers, where erosion during the wet season served to expose fresh rock. Some specimens were actually cored under water because the rocks tend to disintegrate rapidly when exposed to weath- ering. Geology. Very small grains are unstable, but the stability increases as the grain size increases until a critical blocking diameter is reached above which the hematite possesses a very stable magnetization. During the 1962 field season specimens were collected from red horizons of Ecca age (lower Permian) from the Galula coalfield, the Songwe-Kiwira coalfield, and the Ketewaka-Mchuchuma coalfield. Farther to the south in Africa the rocks of Ecca age do not contain red horizons, and attempts to obtain paleomagnetic information for this region have been unsuccessful [Nairn, 1960; Graham, 1961]. Field work was severely limited by the lack of roads, which limited accessibility to outcrops. Artificial exposures such as road cuts and quar- ries are practically nonexistent. The most useful exposures proved to be the beds of dry rivers, where erosion during the wet season served to expose fresh rock. Some specimens were actually cored under water because the rocks tend to disintegrate rapidly when exposed to weath- ering. Geology. It has long been maintained by southern hemisphere geologists that during the Ecca stage of the Karroo sys- tem southern Africa lay in high latitudes. The reason for this contention is that the Ecca is the rock unit which is deposited on the glacial tillires, varves, and glacial pavements of the Dwyka glacial horizon. The reality and inten- sity of the Dwyka glaciation in Africa has sel- dom been questioned and is well documented [du Toit, 1954; Flint, 1961]. The Dwyka gla- ciation is remarkably extensive, and glacial tills and varvites have been recorded from the Congo, Southern Rhodesia, Northern Rhodesia, Tanganyika, and South-West Africa, as well as from the well-known localities of the Republic of South Africa. Om)¾xE  Physics Department University College o/Rhodesia and Nyasaland Salisbury, Southern Rhodesia Abstract. Samples have been collected from twelve sites in red horizons of lower Permian (Ecca) age in southwest Tanganyika. Two directions of magnetization are observed, one steeply inclined with north-seeking poles down and the other with south-seeking poles down in the direction of the earth's present magnetic field. Specimens from all the sites were sub- jected to both alternating-field and thermal demagnetization. These laboratory studies show that the component which is north-seeking down with steep inclination is the stable direction of magnetization. It is suggested that the component aligned along the earth's present field is due to the growth of hematite (CRM) in this field. After treatment at temperatures of 300øC, specimens from nine of the twelve sites gave well-grouped directions of magnetization. On the assumption of a geocentric axial dipole field, the mean pole position is at 38.2øS, 64.9øE (A95 = 16ø). This pole position places southern and eastern Africa in temperate or cold- temperate climatic zones, which is in accord with the available paleoclimati½ evidence. The polarity (reversed) of the Ecca of southwest Tanganyika is in accord with all other Permian rocks that have previously been studied. Introduction. section_candidates.excerpt: eserved in basins down- faulted into the Precambrian basement rocks. The biggest of these is the Ruhuhu basin (3 in Figure 1), which contains the type section of the Tanganyika Karroo. In the Ruhuhu basin  Now at Lamont Geological Observatory, Palis- ades, New York. the Karroo rocks have been divided into eight rock units ranging in time from Dwyka (upper PennsyIvanian) to Beaufort (upper Triassic) [Stockley, 1932; Stockley and Oates, 1931]. These eight rock units are designated K1 through K8. This paper deals with the K3 known in the type area (Ketewaka-Mchu- chuma coalfield of the Ruhuhu basin) as the Intermediate marls and sandstones. The relationship of the Red Sandstone formation with the overlying Batoka basalts is not clear, but an unconformity may be present.

The discrep- ancy between the revised Devonian pole for Britain and Devonian data from other parts of Europe, notably Russia, is noted. Introduction. Red beds have been exten- sively used in paleomagnetic research. However, the age of their natural remanent magnetiza- tion (NRM) is often unknown because it is possible that this might be a chemical remanent magnetization and therefore younger than the geological age of the rocks. world's rocks are magnetized normally, that is, in directions consistent with the earth's dipole moment in its present sense, and that the other 50% are reversely magnetized, in directions consistent with a reversed dipole moment of the earth~ There are apparently only two possible explanations of the reversed magnetizations, namely either (i) that for approximately 50% of geological time the earth's dipole moment has actually been reversed (field reversal), or (if) that the reversely magnetized specimens pos- sess, or have possessed, some intrinsic proper- ty which has either enabled them to become magnetized in directions opposite to those of the ambient fields in which they were laid down, or has enabled normal magnetizations to reverse at some time subsequent to their acquisition (self- reversal) [1, 2], The evidence for and against field reversal and self-reversal has been reviewed by Wil- son [3, 4]° In favour of the predominance of field reversal is the evidence from baked con- tacts [3-5], reversals "caught in the act" [6-13] and the dating of polarity epochs [9, 14-23]. On the other hand petrological differences between normal and reversed specimens [24-30] suggest the possibility of self-reversal. Few systematic differences in the magnetic proper

[24-30] suggest the possibility of self-reversal. Few systematic differences in the magnetic properties of normal and reversed specimens have yet been discov- ered, apart from the directions of the NRMs. A paradox not yet resolved is that certain rock se- quences which exhibit petrological differences between normal and reversed specimens (sug- gesting self-reversal) also produce independent evidence of field reversal [4, 30]. 2. Mauk, and Rob Van der Voo Department of Geological Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109 Abstract. For a palcomagnetic study of the Upper Cretaceous of the Netherlands Leeward Antilles, we have analyzed 187 oriented samples from the complex norite-tonalite batholith and the diabase-schist-tuff formation on Aruba and 44 oriented samples from various igneous units of the Washikemba Formation on Bonaire. Both alternating field and thermal demagnetization procedures were used to demagnetize the samples. Most of the cores yielded univeetorial Zijderveld diagrams above 10-20 mT or 400 ø C. Virtual geomagnetic poles calculated from site means were then compared with equiva- lently aged poles for eratonic South America and other Caribbean sites. The Washikemba Formation of Bonaire and the diabase-schist-tuff formation of Aruba yield poles that are similar to those of Guajira (Colombia) and the Caribbean Mountains of northern Venezuela, whereas they are rotated ap- proximately 90 ø with respect to the pole for stable South America.

re part of a microplate, the Bonaire Block, which has had complex interactions with the South American and Caribbean macroplates (see Figure 1). If the relative motions of North and South America proposed by Ladd [1976] are correct, then the evolution of the southern Caribbean involved convergent and divergent as well as transcurrent motions. Both Aruba and Bonaire are characterized by radiometrically and paleontologieally dated epi- sodes of igneous activity from the Albian through the Paleocene and thus are well suited for a palco- magnetic investigation of possible latitudinal and/or rotational tectonics associated with the Bonaire Block. Previously published palcomagnetic work on similarly aged rocks from other parts of the Bonaire Block include data from the Guajira Peninsula of Colombia [MacDonald and Opdyke, 1972] and the Caribbean Mountains of northern Venezuela [Skerlec and Hargraves, 1980]. Both studies yield palcomag- netic directions with equatorial or subequatorial pole positions for the microplate and rotated appro- ximately 90  away from calculated mean poles for contemporaneous cratonic regions of both North and Copyright 1982 by the American Geophysical Union. Skerlec and Hargraves suggest that the increasing number of consistent palcomag- netic results derived from widely separated sites within the Caribbean realm combined with the pro- bable short duration of a magnetic reversal [MeE1- hinny, 1973] indicates that tectonic rotation is a more likely explanation of the data. Our study involved 231 samples from 24 sites in Late Cretaceous and early Tertiary rocks from Aruba and Bonaire. We interpret the data as additional support for an approximately 90 ø rotation of the Bonaire Block or at least segments of that block. Furthermore, we suggest that our data are evidence for a clockwise sense to the rotation. However, the north- easterly direction yielded by the Aruban batholith, which we interpret to be a Late Cretaceous/early Paleocene direction, is intermediate between an easterly (rotated) direction and an unrotated northerly direction. Because of this, we argue that the paleomagnetic data suggest a clockwise ro- tation. One big problem with this interpretation is that three felsic dikes (sites 4, 8B, and 9B), which cut the batholith and must therefore be younger, apparently carry what we consider to be the earlier Cretaceous direction. Two explanations are possible. If all the magnetizations are primary, then our data would support a three-phase rotational history for the Bonaire Block. More specifically, they would sug- gest a clockwise rotation followed by a counter- clockwise rotation which in turn was followed by a clockwise rotation. In many cases, however, the primary magnetic direction will be changed or masked by later magnetization during the later history of the rock . There are many different ways in which rocks are remagnetized (see Cox and Doell, 1960). As pointed out by Graham and others (1957), one of the most important ways in which the remagneti­ zation of igneous rocks takes place is magnetostriction - or the magnetizing effect of stress. Quite commonly late chemical changes , like weathering , introduce secondary remanent magnetization in rocks (Nagata, 1961). Bulk remanent magnetization, which is measurable with a sensitive magnetometer, may thus be composed of many components of different origin. Usually , we are interested only in the most primary magnetization of a rock. Fortunately , later magnetization can in some cases be removed by »cleaning» rock specimens by me ans of partial demagnetization. This is possible when the primary magnetization is more stable than the later components. This demagnetization is done in an alternating magnetic field of sufficient strength (Brynjolfsson , 1957; As and Zijderveld , 1958 ; and Creer, 1959), or by heating the specimens in a magnetically zero field to an elevated temperature (Irving and others , 1961; and Chamalaun and Creer 1964). The haematite, which does not as a rule exceed 5% by volume, occurs as discrete grains and gran- ular aggregates as well as around grain boundaries in interstitial cement. Accessory minerals include green biotite, muscovite, sericite, chlorite and partly altered feldspar (mainly andesine). The samples from Cakraz and Tarlagzi (T013-T026) are character- ised by the presence of abundant interstitial calcite and some calcite veins, no doubt partly derived by infiltration from the Barremian limestone above. The Tarlagzi samples contain in addition some detrital calcite and frag- ments of what appear to be organic structures. The haematite grains of TOl~TOl5 are larger and less numerous than those of T016-T018; it is possible that the difference in magnetic properties between these two groups of samples (of which more below) is related to this observation. In the Aritdere samples (T027-T031), calcite is not nearly so abundant as in those from the other two localities. The Aritdere location lies some kilometers from the nearest outcrop of the Barremian; having presumably been longer exposed, the sandstones here have perhaps lost again much of their calcite to infiltrating rain water. is presented. In Scotland the relative ages of the dikes could be determined with some accuracy by the strata they intruded. In the Canadian Shield area, with one exception, there are no overlying strata to permit classification, so it is necessary to resort to other, less ob- vious criteria for classification. The most useful of these is the strike of the dike in relation to that of other dikes, but this is not always adequate, as swarms of different ages may have the same strikes. Anderson (1951) has made a thorough study of the dikes of Scotland and the mechanics of their intrusion. He points out that dikes tend to have a fairly constant width and to be equally spaced. This means that width and separation may also be useful criteria for dike classification. One other method of classification has been a careful study of composition, a cri- terion useful in only a few particular cases. The usual classification is one where we have olivine diabase, quartz diabase, or simple diabase. In the process of crystallization of diabasic magma it has been found that oli- vine and quartz are mutually exclusive, and it is supposed that the dikes of various com- positions are formed from different magmas. In the Canadian Shield area, with one exception, there are no overlying strata to permit classification, so it is necessary to resort to other, less ob- vious criteria for classification. The most useful of these is the strike of the dike in relation to that of other dikes, but this is not always adequate, as swarms of different ages may have the same strikes. Anderson (1951) has made a thorough study of the dikes of Scotland and the mechanics of their intrusion. He points out that dikes tend to have a fairly constant width and to be equally spaced. This means that width and separation may also be useful criteria for dike classification. One other method of classification has been a careful study of composition, a cri- terion useful in only a few particular cases. The usual classification is one where we have olivine diabase, quartz diabase, or simple diabase. DIKE SWARMS OF NORTHWEST QUEBEC AND NORTHEAST ONTARIO In the Precambrian Shield of Quebec and Ontario there are several well-developed dike swarms. In parts of the area, in partic- ular the commercially significant greenstone belts, detailed geologic mapping has been done. Recently, wide-scale aeromagnetic surveys have been carried out, showing the presence of a large number of dikes. In the present study a careful compilation of all reported dike exposures and all published airborne magnetic data of a portion of On- tario and Quebec has been made. In the maps accompanying this paper (figs. 1, 2) the compiled data are presented. It can be seen quite clearly that there are several dif- ferent dike swarms with different strike di- rections. The dikes are discussed by Norman (1948), by Moore (1955), by Gill and L'Es- perance (1952) and in the reports of the On- tario Department of Mines, the Quebec Bureau of Mines, and the Geological Survey of Canada. These directions of magnetization were determined from the samples after they were magnetically washed in an a-c. field of 80 or 130 oersteds. The reasons for the dispersion within the individual swarms are discussed. The pole positions of the Sudbury and Mackenzie dykes are almost identical and the two swarms are the same age within the limits of analytical uncertainty. However, basalt of the Sudbury swarm is alkalic and more undersaturated than basalt of the Mackenzie dykes. He found that its magnetization was parallel to that of the dyke itself and concluded from this that the stable direction of magnetization in the dykes is parallel to the earth's field at the time of intrusion and is not controlled by some demagnetization process operating within the cooling dyke. We have collected 45 samples from the sites shown on Fig. 2. Thirty-seven of these samples were stable and their magnetic vectors are shown on Fig. 6. SAMPLE COLLECTION AND MEASUREMENT Six hundred and fifty oriented samples were collected from about 350 sites in the initial phase of the program; 225 of these samples are from the six swarms discussed in this report. At each site an attempt was made to collect at least two samples. It would have been desirable to collect more oriented samples at each site, but the additional time required would have meant that the swarms could not have been sampled throughout, a requirement for a concurrent systematic geochemical and petrographic study of the swarms. Two 1-in. cubes were cut from each sample and their magnetization was determined with either a spinner or astatic magnetometer. To eliminate the viscous component of magnetization usually present in igneous rocks, all cubes were subjected to an alternating field whose peak value was empirically set at 80 or 130 oersteds. Since the apparatus (Larochelle 1962) used in this operation did not allow tumbling of the specimens during treatment, the demagnetizing procedure was repeated three times with the three axes of the cube successively aligned parallel wit11 the axis of the demagnetizing coil. Barron and Sioux Quartzites The Barron quartzite of Wisconsin is in most places a fine-grained, flesh-pink, well- bedded rock, almost wholly of quartz. Cross- bedding is rare, and folding and faulting are gentle, the dips being usually less than 12°. The Sioux Quartzite of Minnesota is thought to be equivalent. It crops out in the Minnesota valley in a series of terraces along the north wall, where it consists of red quartzite, sand- stones, and conglomerates. Samples were taken in four localities, and the stereograms of the results are shown in Figure 2 (A-D). The exposures at each of the localities are poor, and the specimens too few to produce symmetrically grouped stereograms. The Sioux and Barren quartzites from Minnesota and Wisconsin, the Uinta Moun- tain Group from Utah, and the Apache Group from southern Arizona give poles in the east-central equatorial Pacific similar to those of the Grand Canyon Series from northern Arizona and the Belt Series from Montana. It crops out in the Minnesota valley in a series of terraces along the north wall, where it consists of red quartzite, sand- stones, and conglomerates. Samples were taken in four localities, and the stereograms of the results are shown in Figure 2 (A-D). The exposures at each of the localities are poor, and the specimens too few to produce symmetrically grouped stereograms. In spite of this, the mean directions at the different sites are in reasonable agreement. Thus one can conclude that the magnetization is pre- dominantly due to a single component, which, being significantly different from the present dipole field, is likely to be an original mag- netization. Goldich and others (1961) date the Sioux Quartzite as at least 1 billion years, but think it is very much older; therefore the paleomag- netic results, though meager, are of consider- able interest. The absence in this region of complicated tectonic movements enables one to correct paleomagnetic measurements on even the oldest formations for geological tilt with confidence. Also, compared with many other regions, such as the Appalachians, there is little chance that the rocks have acquired a secondary component of magnetization after formation as the result of stresses during tectonic activity. Further, the presence of numerous unmetamorphosed Precambrian red beds in the western States make possible a sufficient sampling of paleomagnetic directions for any trend to emerge in this long interval of geological time. For each formation, the extensive exposures enable one to make a fair sampling throughout its entire vertical extent. A decrease in intensity of the magnetization without change in direction is bound to occur through thermal fluctuation in the domains of the magnetized iron oxide grains and is of no consequence for this work. A symmetrical grouping of directions, signif- icantly different from the present dipole field, shows that the remanent magnetization has not been acquired in the last million years. A markedly asymmetrical grouping suggests the presence of primary and secondary magnetiza- tions and precludes any conclusion being drawn concerning the paleofield, until the components can be separated by demagnetiza- tion experiments or by other means. In the former case if metamorphism has not occurred, it is legitimate to postulate that the original magnetizations were acquired at the time of deposition or within a geological period of this time. This may best be tested by the com- parison of formations of similar age within one continent.
